name: Acidic or extreme substrate-pH root stress
summary: A measured root-zone condition in which persistently acidic peat-based substrate suppresses Cannabis shoot and root development, while either acidic or high-pH extremes can restrict visible root growth. There is no unique leaf appearance: cultivar, fertility, EC, substrate, and exposure duration materially change what a camera can see.
affectedParts: root tips and developing root system
lower foliage when low pH is combined with excessive micronutrient fertility in a susceptible cultivar
leaf tips and leaflet interior during treatment-associated bronzing and necrosis
root-zone solution and substrate for direct pH and EC measurement
indicators: Repeated calibrated substrate measurements remain at an extreme rather than a single irrigation or runoff reading
Root-tip development is reduced relative to matched healthy plants before a specific foliar pattern is reliable
Visible root-tip counts can be reduced at both acidic and high-pH extremes even when intermediate treatments remain similar
Whole-plant diameter and accumulated shoot biomass lag despite plant height sometimes remaining similar
At acidic pH, leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations may rise without visible toxicity
Termination EC can also rise at pH extremes, so pH exposure must be interpreted with simultaneous salinity and fertility measurements
In the Sweetened pH 3.8 plus fourfold-micronutrient treatment, lower-leaf tips bronzed, became necrotic, spread inward, and developed chlorosis
The same low-pH and high-micronutrient treatment did not produce the same foliage response in Cherry Wine
exclusions: Only nutrient-solution input pH was measured and the actual substrate or root-zone pH is unknown
A single runoff, reservoir, or slurry reading is outside target but repeat representative measurements are not
High EC, fertilizer imbalance, or source-water alkalinity explains the response without a persistent measured substrate-pH extreme
Roots are restricted by saturation, compaction, container binding, drought, temperature, oxygen limitation, transplant damage, or root disease
Foliar bronzing or necrosis is localized to heat, light, spray, contact, pest feeding, or infectious lesions
Tissue analysis supports a specific nutrient deficiency or toxicity and measured root-zone pH is not outside the production-system target
Color differences appear only under altered lighting, white balance, cultivar pigmentation, senescence, or compression artifact

A detached root, leaf, cropped panel, composite, or canopy image is assigned to a pH, EC, tissue, or treatment result without a persistent plant and specimen identifier linking the photographed organ, sampling location, exposure history, collection event, and report

The study-specific pH 3.0, 3.1, 3.8, 4.0, 5.0, 5.5, 5.9, 6.5, 7.0, or 7.1 values; 21-day timing; root-tip counts; tissue concentrations; growth response; or cultivar phenotype is used as a universal diagnostic threshold, timing rule, production target, or severity prediction
A generic nutrient-availability chart or expected lockout is treated as proof of a specific deficiency or toxicity without linked root-zone, input, tissue, and plant-response evidence

progression.description: Substrate pH persists outside the intended system range; solution pH alone does not establish the root-zone exposure.

Preserve plant, chamber, observation-window, scale, and date identity across captures; record which roots are visible and the counting rule. This annotation protocol follows the study measurement limits, not a validated camera diagnostic. Do not infer hidden root volume or biomass from a wall view.
Root-tip expansion can slow before a diagnostic foliage pattern appears. In Baox, separation at pH 3.1 and 7.1 was evident by 21 days after planting.

Plant diameter or shoot dry mass can fall while height remains deceptively similar. Keep these endpoints separate from wall-visible root length and tip counts; a root-window image does not measure total root biomass.
Low pH plus excessive micronutrients may cause lower-leaf tip bronzing, chlorosis, and spreading necrosis in a susceptible cultivar, but absence of those symptoms does not exclude pH stress.
New root tips, canopy expansion, and new-leaf quality should be followed over time; existing necrosis will not reverse and response alone does not prove the original diagnosis.

Study Figures 4 and 5 are five-week vegetative treatment comparisons, not serial frames of one plant. Figure 6 documents lower-leaf progression in Sweetened under excess micronutrients; it is not a pure low-pH syndrome.

Experiment 1 Table 4 did not show a significant phosphorus difference across the tested pH treatments. Do not infer phosphorus lockout from a chart or leaf color; retain linked tissue analysis and medium-specific exposure evidence.

Preserve lime composition alongside pH: calcium supply changed with liming. Retain iron treatment means and significance groups; the numerical peak at pH 5.0 does not establish a monotonic image label.

Experiment 3 kept recently matured upper-third leaves separate from older lower leaves. For confirmation, retain canopy position, leaf age, collection date, and specimen ID with each assay and image; do not assign an upper-leaf result to a lower-leaf photograph. Roots were discarded, so these leaf assays cannot confirm root mineral status.

Figure 6 uses an iron-bronzing caption, but Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, and Mo varied together and the discussion does not establish iron accumulation. Keep visible bronzing, mixed-micronutrient exposure, measured pH, and iron-specific causality as separate labels. Obtain matched tissue and exposure evidence before attributing the image to one element.

For serial image or video comparisons, retain pot-rim-to-apex height and widest and perpendicular canopy spans as separate measurements with units, plant ID, capture date, camera orientation and in-plane scale. Pair side and top views with calibrated pH and EC from that plant and a same-cultivar control. These are dataset capture safeguards inferred from Experiment 1 measurement landmarks, not a validated image-to-biomass conversion or a universal pH classifier.

confirmation: Assign separate labels for measured pH exposure, visible injury, nutrient status, salinity or fertility context, root-growth response, and causally attributed pH stress; a meter reading alone does not establish that pH caused the photographed injury.

Link repeated pH and EC readings, root views, canopy images, cultivar, and intervention dates to the same persistent plant identifier; do not transfer measurements from neighboring plants or pooled substrate to an individual image label.

Assign persistent plant, root-zone sample, root specimen, and leaf-tissue identifiers before capture or collection, and carry them through images or video, sampling method and location, treatment history, calibration records, laboratory reports, and follow-up observations.
Do not diagnose pH stress from leaf color, tip burn, stunting, one photograph, one video, or a generic nutrient-availability chart.

Measure the actual substrate or root-zone pH repeatedly with a calibrated meter, appropriate standards, and one documented method for the medium; do not compare PourThru, saturated-media-extract, 1:2 dilution, runoff, reservoir, or direct-probe values as though they were interchangeable.

For container substrates, sample multiple representative containers and preserve each reading before averaging; record sampling location, depth, irrigation timing, extraction volume, equilibration or drainage time, meter calibration, temperature, substrate moisture, and replicate values.

Measure root-zone and input EC alongside pH, and document source-water pH and alkalinity, fertilizer formulation, acid or base additions, lime charge, substrate batch, irrigation volume, leaching fraction, and drainage.

Capture serial whole-plant top and side views, root-zone and cleaned-root views, upper- and lower-canopy views, and close-ups of both leaf surfaces under repeatable lighting with scale and a matched same-cultivar control.

Record cultivar, plant age, stage, days of exposure, container volume, substrate composition, water content, root-zone temperature, dissolved oxygen where relevant, and root-tip quantity or standardized root coverage.

Use representative leaf-tissue and root-zone or substrate analysis to separate a pH-associated exposure from a specific nutrient disorder; use a plant diagnostic laboratory when discolored or decaying roots, lesions, or pests remain plausible.
Retain a measured-exposure or suspected label unless the pH history, root or growth response, competing exposures, and analytical evidence are linked to the photographed plant.

For agricultural soil, retain the laboratory lime-requirement or exchangeable-acidity method, soil class, amendment identity and rate, application date, particle fineness or effective neutralizing value, incorporation depth, and a map linking sampled locations to photographed plants. A portable pH reading is not a lime-dose calculation.
immediateActions: Preserve pre-correction pH, EC, alkalinity, solution, substrate, tissue, root, and image records before changing the system.
Verify the measuring method and calibration with repeat samples; avoid large unmeasured acid, base, lime, fertilizer, or flush corrections.
Quarantine uncertain images and videos from diagnostic ground truth until exposure and confounder evidence is linked.
correctivePlan: Correct the verified cause gradually using substrate- and water-appropriate guidance, considering alkalinity and buffering rather than input pH alone.
Restore a balanced fertilizer and irrigation program while monitoring substrate pH, EC, water content, drainage, and new root growth.
Reassess root pathogens, salinity, water status, temperature, and nutrient-specific differentials if new root tips and growth do not improve after the measured pH returns to the intended range.

For a field-soil case, obtain a soil-laboratory amendment recommendation with its method and crop/soil assumptions before changing lime supply. Preserve measured spatial differences and previous amendment placement rather than extrapolating one surface reading to the entire root zone.
prevention: Establish a production-system-specific substrate pH and EC monitoring protocol with calibrated meters, consistent extraction methods, replicate sampling, and trend alerts.
Test source-water alkalinity and account for substrate lime and fertilizer acidity before making recurring pH adjustments.
Keep same-cultivar controls and serial root and canopy images so gradual growth restriction is not mistaken for a specific leaf disorder.
warnings: The 0.15 image/video-only ceiling is an annotation safeguard, not measured diagnostic accuracy; cameras cannot measure substrate pH or establish causality.
Stable old necrosis after a correction is not ongoing pH injury, and apparent recovery does not exclude simultaneous salt, water, nutrient, or pathogen problems.
The study supports a measured substrate-pH stress record, not a universal image phenotype or a universal nutrient-lockout chart.
The 5.5 to 6.5 recommendation came from peat-based greenhouse experiments and must not be copied unchanged to soil, field, coco, rockwool, aeroponic, or deep-water systems.
At normal micronutrient supply, low pH increased tissue accumulation without a universal visible toxicity; absence of bronzing does not establish that the root zone is acceptable.
The lower-leaf bronzing sequence occurred in Sweetened under pH 3.8 plus fourfold micronutrients and was absent in Cherry Wine; it is not low-pH-specific ground truth.
A single runoff or reservoir pH value does not prove the pH experienced throughout the root system.

Extraction method, substrate moisture, sampling location, equilibration or drainage time, calibration, and crop-specific interpretation materially affect pH and EC results; general greenhouse ranges are not Cannabis thresholds.
The Purdue source is a cross-crop measurement protocol. Its non-Cannabis figures and general EC ranges are not diagnostic media or direct Cannabis response evidence.

One PDF-located figure candidate is indexed as metadata only; original image bytes, visual content, exact license version and item-level credits remain unverified. No image or video is admitted for display or training.
All symptom-only, uncalibrated-pH, mixed-method, or plant-unlinked samples remain low confidence and require human review.

The NC State source is a general agricultural-soil guide, not a Cannabis diagnostic trial. Its crop targets, Ac-value equation, application rates, and amendment time courses must not be transferred to container or hydroponic systems; the added sampling safeguards are annotation inferences, not validated visual classifiers.

sources.title: Impact of substrate pH and micronutrient fertility rates on Cannabis sativa
sources.publisher: Wiley Periodicals LLC on behalf of the Crop Science Society of America and the American Society of Agronomy
supportedClaims: In a controlled peat-perlite experiment, industrial hemp shoot dry weight was lower at substrate pH 3.0 and 4.0 than at pH 5.0 through 7.0; plant diameter was smaller at pH 3.0, while mean plant height did not differ across that pH range.
Visible root-tip counts in Cannabis sativa Baox mini-rhizotrons were lowest at both measured extremes, pH 3.1 and 7.1, by 21 days after planting, while counts at pH 3.7 through 5.9 were similar.
Termination EC was higher at pH 3.0 and 7.0 than at intermediate pH values in the first experiment, so pH response cannot be interpreted without the accompanying salt and fertility context.

Lower pH increased several leaf-tissue micronutrient concentrations, but normal micronutrient supply did not produce a universal toxicity phenotype; the authors concluded that Cannabis growth was inhibited below pH 5.0 and recommended a greenhouse substrate range of 5.5 to 6.5 for the systems evaluated.

With fourfold micronutrients at target pH 3.8, Sweetened developed lower-foliage tip bronzing that advanced to necrosis, inward spread, and chlorosis, whereas Cherry Wine did not show the same response, demonstrating cultivar- and fertility-dependent appearance.

The experiments evaluated peat-based greenhouse substrates and four cultivars across separate experiments: Baox, T1, Cherry Wine, and Sweetened. Their pH values, timing, tissue concentrations, and symptom expression are treatment-specific and do not establish universal soil, coco, rockwool, or hydroponic thresholds.

Experiment 2 measured the five longest wall-visible roots per chamber and counted visible root tips at 6 to 21 days after planting; roots inside the substrate were not measured. These endpoints are not total root biomass.

Figures 4 and 5 compare Cherry Wine and Sweetened, respectively, after five weeks of vegetative growth; they are treatment comparisons, whereas Figure 6 shows the Sweetened lower-foliage bronzing progression under fourfold micronutrients.

In Experiment 1 Table 4, leaf phosphorus did not differ significantly across target pH 3.0 to 7.0; this peat-perlite result does not validate a phosphorus-lockout diagnosis from a generic field-soil availability chart.

Experiment 1 used calcium-containing lime to establish pH treatments; the authors related rising tissue calcium to lime availability. The pH and calcium-supply changes cannot be treated as independent causes.

Experiment 1 Table 5 reported the highest numerical leaf iron concentration at target pH 5.0, not 3.0; the two means shared a significance letter. A general low-pH accumulation trend is not a monotonic iron classifier.

Experiment 3 analyzed recently matured upper-third leaves separately from older lower leaves at the five-week harvest; remaining shoots were harvested separately and roots discarded. Its leaf assays are not root assays.
Experiment 3 Table 2 increased Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, and Mo together across micronutrient treatments; the bronzing treatment was not an isolated iron challenge.

Although Figure 6 calls the appearance iron bronzing, the discussion describes lower-leaf iron values as similar to a prior survey and suggests Cannabis is not an iron accumulator under these conditions; the caption alone does not establish iron-specific toxicity.

Experiment 1 measured height from the pot rim to the apical meristem and recorded canopy diameter using widest and perpendicular dimensions at the final harvest. Dataset inference: preserve landmarks and both spans; apparent pixel height or canopy area is not the reported growth endpoint or proof of pH injury.

sources.title: pH and Electrical Conductivity Measurements in Soilless Substrates
sources.organization: Purdue University Extension, Department of Horticulture and Landscape Architecture
supportedClaims: The institutional protocol treats substrate pH and electrical conductivity as separate measurements: pH affects nutrient availability, while EC represents dissolved salts; irrigation-water alkalinity, substrate analysis, and plant-tissue analysis provide additional information that neither meter value supplies alone.

Accepted soilless-substrate extraction methods include PourThru, saturated media extract, and 1:2 dilution; each has a distinct procedure and method-dependent interpretation, so values from different methods must not be pooled as interchangeable thresholds.

A monitoring program should use calibrated pH and conductivity standards, repeat a consistent extraction method, sample multiple representative containers separately, and interpret their average and trend with crop, substrate, fertilizer, irrigation-water, and production records.

Directly inserting a probe into substrate is not recommended unless moisture content and sampling timing are tightly standardized; the saturated-media method instead samples the interior root zone and avoids the top and bottom inch because salt concentration may differ there.

This greenhouse protocol is not Cannabis-specific and supports measurement quality and exclusion checks only; its general crop ranges and pictured non-Cannabis disorders are not Cannabis diagnostic thresholds or media ground truth.

sources.title: Soil Acidity and Liming for Agricultural Soils
sources.organization: NC State Extension Publications, SoilFacts AG-439-50
supportedClaims: The Soil Testing section distinguishes soil pH from exchangeable acidity (the NCDA&CS Ac value); a portable pH reading alone cannot determine an accurate agricultural-soil lime requirement. This supports a measurement safeguard, not a Cannabis amendment dose.

The Liming Materials section relates lime effectiveness to calcium-carbonate equivalent and particle fineness; the Application and Incorporation section describes limited movement and uneven spreading that can leave underlimed or overlimed strips. Amendment placement is therefore relevant context for spatial soil sampling.

The guide differentiates mineral, mineral-organic, and organic soils and crop-specific targets; its North Carolina field-soil targets and lime equations are not universal Cannabis, peat-container, coco, rockwool, or hydroponic guidance.
